tur43-6: Bone is a living tissue that is constantly broken down and rebuilt. With age, and in women especially after menopause, breakdown happens faster than rebuilding; bone density falls and the internal structure thins. As a result, a simple fall or strains such as bending forward to lift a load can cause a fracture. The spine, hip and wrist are the most common sites.
tur43-7: The diagnosis is made by measuring bone density (DEXA) (see Diagnosis and T-score). Your physician decides who should have a scan and when, based on risk factors.
tur43-8: Diagnosis: bone density scan and T-score
tur43-9: Bone density is most often assessed with a short scan called DEXA; usually the top of the thigh bone and the lumbar spine are measured. The result is compared with the average for young adults and given as a T-score. According to the World Health Organization definition reported by the International Osteoporosis Foundation, the T-score measured at the neck of the thigh bone is interpreted as follows:
tur43-17: T-score of −2.5 or lower and at least one fragility fracture.
tur43-18: DEXA measures the amount of bone, not its quality. Most people who have a fragility fracture do not have a T-score below −2.5; in other words, most fractures occur in people at the osteopenia level. This is why fracture risk is also estimated with calculators such as FRAX, which assess bone density together with age, previous fractures and other risk factors. Because results from different machines can differ, follow-up scans are preferably done on the same machine. Your physician interprets the result.
tur43-20: Postmenopausal osteoporosis was described in the 1940s. In recent years the place of exercise in bone health has become clearer; recommendations have widened from walking alone to muscle strengthening, balance and movement that protects the spine.
tur43-21: Fuller Albright and colleagues published their paper describing the clinical features of postmenopausal osteoporosis in JAMA.
tur43-22: Researchers and clinicians from Australia, Canada, Finland and the United States, in partnership with Osteoporosis Canada, published the Too Fit To Fracture exercise recommendations (Osteoporosis International): a multicomponent programme including resistance and balance exercise was strongly recommended, and it was stressed that people should not do aerobic exercise alone while neglecting resistance and balance training.
tur43-23: The LIFTMOR trial (JBMR): in 101 postmenopausal women with low bone density, 30 minutes of supervised high-intensity resistance and impact training twice a week clearly increased lumbar spine bone density at 8 months compared with a group doing low-intensity home exercise.
tur43-24: The UK National Osteoporosis Society (now the Royal Osteoporosis Society) published its "Strong, Steady and Straight" expert consensus statement: muscle strengthening 2–3 days a week, about 50 impacts on most days for those suitable, balance exercises and movement that protects the spine.
tur43-25: The UK osteoporosis guideline (NOGG) was updated: it stressed that the risk of a new fracture is especially high in the period right after a fracture, and the importance of timely referral or drug treatment where needed.
tur43-26: A review of 69 trials (BMJ): in adults not taking osteoporosis medication, calcium and vitamin D supplements did not reduce fractures or falls to a clinically meaningful degree; it was noted that the result may not apply to people with specific bone disorders or those taking osteoporosis medication.
tur43-27: The expert consensus statement of the UK National Osteoporosis Society (now called the Royal Osteoporosis Society, ROS) groups exercise around three goals: strengthening bone, preventing falls and protecting the spine.
tur43-28: 2–3 days a week; over time, build up to 3 sets of 8–12 repetitions for each exercise. Including exercises that strengthen the back muscles is also recommended.
tur43-29: For those suitable, about 50 moderate impacts on most days, for example light jogging steps or small jumps, are recommended. For people with a history of a spinal fracture or more than one fracture, lower-impact activities rather than moderate impacts are recommended as a general rule; for frail people with limited mobility, low-impact activity such as walking for up to 20 minutes a day.
tur43-30: In postmenopausal women with low bone density, supervised high-intensity resistance and impact training clearly increased spinal bone density at 8 months compared with a group doing low-intensity home exercise. Programmes like this need to be planned for the individual and carried out under supervision.
tur43-31: Needs for medication, calcium and vitamin D vary from person to person; your physician decides on these. In a review of 69 trials published in The BMJ in 2026, calcium and vitamin D supplements did not reduce fractures or falls to a clinically meaningful degree in adults not taking osteoporosis medication; the researchers note that the result may not apply to people with specific bone disorders or those taking osteoporosis medication. Do not stop a supplement you have been advised to take on your own; ask your physician which is suitable for you. Stopping smoking and limiting alcohol also help protect your bones.
tur43-32: Exercise recommendations: two sources side by side
tur43-33: The expert consensus statement of the UK National Osteoporosis Society (now called the Royal Osteoporosis Society, ROS) (2018) and the Too Fit To Fracture recommendations prepared in partnership with Osteoporosis Canada (2014), side by side. Both are based on expert opinion and the available studies; the programme is adjusted to the person, their fracture history and general health.

tur43-37: Progressive resistance exercise for all major muscle groups at least twice a week; 2 sets with at least one exercise for each muscle group, 8–12 repetitions if suitable. People who are inactive can start at a lower level.
tur43-38: Balance and strengthening exercises for people over 65 and those with balance problems.
tur43-39: Balance training every day; about 2 hours a week (15–20 minutes a day).
tur43-41: For those suitable, about 50 moderate impacts on most days; for people with a history of a spinal fracture or more than one fracture, lower-impact activities as a general rule.
tur43-42: A target of 150–300 minutes of moderate or 75–150 minutes of vigorous aerobic activity a week, but not instead of resistance and balance exercise; for people with a spinal fracture, shorter or lower-intensity activities may be more suitable.
tur43-43: Movements that involve bending the spine forward for long periods, to the end of the range or under load are modified.
tur43-44: Care with twisting and bending forward during transitions between movements; people at high risk of spinal fracture avoid resistance machines that require bending forward and twisting, unless it is certain they can use them correctly. tur43-46: For people with a spinal fracture, consulting a physiotherapist is suggested to make sure exercise is safe and appropriate.
tur43-47: Stand up straight holding on to a counter. Lift both heels together and rise onto your toes, hold for 2 seconds and lower slowly. tur43-48: Yes; exercise is one of the most important parts of bone health. The expert consensus statement of the UK National Osteoporosis Society (now the Royal Osteoporosis Society) recommends muscle strengthening, impact exercise for suitable people, and balance training. It is recommended that the type and intensity of exercise be adjusted with a physiotherapist according to your fracture history and general health.
tur43-49: My T-score came out as −2. What does that mean?
tur43-50: According to the World Health Organization definition, a T-score between −1 and −2.5 means osteopenia, that is, low bone mass; for a diagnosis of osteoporosis on DEXA, the T-score needs to be −2.5 or lower. However, most people who have a fragility fracture do not have a T-score below −2.5. This is why fracture risk is estimated not only from the T-score but also with calculators such as FRAX, which assess bone density together with other risk factors; your physician decides whether treatment is needed. In the LIFTMOR trial in postmenopausal women with low bone density (osteopenia or osteoporosis), supervised resistance and impact training increased bone density.
tur43-51: It is recommended that movements involving bending the spine forward for long periods, to the end of the range or under load be modified or replaced with other movements. For example, instead of movements such as sit-ups or reaching to the floor with straight knees, other abdominal and back exercises can be chosen. When picking something up from the floor, bend your knees and hinge from your hips rather than rounding your back.
tur43-52: Walking is very valuable for general health, but on its own it is usually not enough for bones. Muscle-strengthening exercise 2–3 days a week is recommended; for those suitable, about 50 moderate impacts (light jogging steps, small jumps) can be added on most days. People over 65 and those with balance problems are advised to include balance exercises in their programme as well. For people with a history of a spinal fracture or more than one fracture, however, lower-impact activities rather than moderate impacts are recommended as a general rule.
tur43-53: Yes, but the programme should be adapted to you. It is recommended that people with a painful spinal fracture receive reassuring information early on and that referral to a physiotherapist be considered. At first, strengthening, balance and learning safe movement come before impact exercise. According to the UK's 2022 osteoporosis guideline (NOGG), the risk of a new fracture is especially high in the period right after a fracture; ask your physician whether drug treatment is suitable for you.
tur43-54: In some people it can, under expert supervision. In a trial of 101 postmenopausal women with low bone density, 30 minutes of high-intensity resistance and impact training twice a week clearly increased lumbar spine bone density at 8 months compared with a group doing low-intensity home exercise; its effect on fractures was not measured in this trial. Programmes like this must, however, be planned for the individual and carried out under supervision, step by step.

tur43-58: Hip pain after a fall and being unable to put weight on the leg, or being unable to get up on your own (it may be a hip fracture)

tur43-61: A deformed or clearly swollen wrist after a fall (it may be a fracture)
tur43-62: New back pain together with a fever or a history of cancer

tur43-68: What is a meniscus tear, how is it recognised, and does every tear need surgery? What does an MRI finding mean, and how effective is exercise? A guideline comparison, a short history, six home exercises and warning signs.
tur43-69: The meniscus is the C-shaped cartilage in the knee that acts as a cushion between the thigh bone and the shin bone. In young people it usually tears when the knee twists; after middle age it usually tears through wear. For tears caused by wear, exercise therapy has been found in studies to be as effective as surgery.
tur43-70: Each knee has two menisci, an inner and an outer one. They spread load, protect the joint and give the knee stability. In young people and athletes, a tear usually happens when the knee twists while the foot is planted; it may occur together with an anterior cruciate ligament injury. After middle age, tears that appear through wear without a clear event are more common and are often an early part of osteoarthritis.
tur43-71: The diagnosis is mostly made from your history and an examination. No single examination test is reliable enough on its own; the findings are assessed together.
tur43-72: Pain when the joint line is pressed, pain or a click when the fully bent knee is rotated and straightened while lying on your back (McMurray test), and pain when standing on one leg with the knee slightly bent (about 20°) and turning the body from side to side (Thessaly test) suggest a meniscus tear. According to data reported in the US physiotherapy guideline, the McMurray test picks up about 55% of tears and joint line tenderness 76%. These tests are carried out by a physician or physiotherapist; do not try them at home.
tur43-74: According to the ESSKA consensus, an MRI is usually not needed as a first-line test when a tear caused by wear is suspected; a knee X-ray is useful to support a diagnosis of osteoarthritis or to detect rare other problems. Seeing a tear on MRI does not show that the tear is the cause of the pain.
tur43-76: ESSKA considers tears that appear after age 35 without a significant injury to be caused by wear (degenerative). Tears that happen with a sudden twist are assessed separately; there may also be a ligament injury, and some can be repaired by stitching.
tur43-77: In a study in Norway of 140 people aged 35–60 with a meniscus tear caused by wear, a 12-week supervised exercise programme was compared with arthroscopic meniscus trimming (partial meniscectomy). After two years there was no clinically relevant difference between the groups; at 3 months, thigh muscle strength had increased more in the exercise group.
tur43-78: In the FIDELITY study in Finland with 146 people, the operation was compared with sham (placebo) surgery; after 1 year, symptoms had eased similarly in both groups.
tur43-79: The guideline from an international expert panel published in the BMJ in 2017 strongly recommends against arthroscopic surgery for knee problems caused by wear (including meniscus tears). The recommendation also applies when there are symptoms such as catching or when the symptoms started suddenly. A truly locked knee that cannot be fully straightened, sports injuries in young people and major trauma fall outside the scope of this recommendation; these are assessed separately by an orthopaedic specialist.
tur43-81: For many years, removing a torn meniscus was a common treatment. Research over the last twenty years has shown that, for tears caused by wear, surgery is not better than exercise.
tur43-82: Fairbank described changes such as narrowing of the joint space and bony ridges at the edges on X-rays of knees whose meniscus had been removed.

In other words, regular home exercise is valuable on its own; sessions can help set up the programme correctly and progress it.

Seeing a tear on MRI also does not show that the tear is the cause of the pain: 61% of people over 50 whose MRI showed a tear had had no knee symptoms at all in the previous month. In situations such as a sudden injury or a locked knee, your physician may decide differently.
tur43-112: For tears caused by wear, studies show that surgery is not better than exercise. tur43-113: Only the outer edge of the meniscus has a blood supply; small tears in this area can heal, whereas tears in the inner part usually do not heal on their own. However, even if the tear remains, pain and function can often improve markedly with exercise.

tur43-124: The rotator cuff is made up of the tendons of four muscles that surround the shoulder joint and let us lift and rotate the arm. Tears mostly appear with age, through wear, and many cause no symptoms at all. For tears not caused by a fall or blow, physiotherapy is the first treatment tried in most patients and is often enough.

tur43-128: Screening studies show that full-thickness tears increase markedly with age and that most do not cause symptoms. This is why a tear seen on MRI does not on its own determine the treatment decision.
tur43-129: In diagnosis, how the tear started (with a clear injury or gradually) matters. The tear is assessed with an examination and, if needed, imaging.

tur43-175: Coldness or paleness in the hand, or widespread numbness in the arm, after a dislocation or blow
tur43-176: Redness, warmth, swelling or severe pain in the shoulder, especially together with a fever or feeling unwell
tur43-177: See a physician without delay, within a few days at the latest:
tur43-178: Being unable to lift the arm, or weakness, after a shoulder dislocation in people over 40
tur43-179: Weakness or being unable to lift the arm that is still present 2 weeks after an injury
tur43-180: New shoulder pain, or an unexplained swelling or lump in the shoulder, in someone with a history of cancer
tur43-181: Numbness or tingling spreading down the arm (it may come from the neck)
